transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Verma (SE), Luca Martinez (Product) — Maya, Samir, Becky, Rajiv (Aperture Labs)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): quick SDK walkthrough, auth pattern Qs, ask about VPC + KMS, plan for bench + repo share, next meeting for private scoping.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, super excited to walk through the SDK quickstart and the environment bits. who all do we have on from Aperture?
[00:07] Maya: Hi, I'm Maya — lead ML at Aperture, we own the RAG pipeline and prompt infra.
[00:11] Samir: Samir here, platform eng. we'll take the integration and infra side.
[00:14] Becky: Becky, dev lead, we'll be shipping the feature in Q4.
[00:18] Rajiv: Rajiv, security, I'll be raising the typical KMS/SSO questions.
[00:22] Jordan: Great, Jordan from Redwood AE, Priya SE will run the demo, Luca is on to answer product questions. We'll keep to about 45 minutes, show Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth, dotenv/CI patterns, then cover Optimize tips and your security asks.

[00:40] Priya: Alright jumping into the quickstart — two repos, python and typescript. the flow is super minimal: set REDWOOD_API_KEY or configure the SSO token, then call client.chat.completions or embeddings.
[00:52] Maya: can you show the streaming example? we do streaming in prod for tokens and partial UI updates.
[00:56] Priya: Yeah, here's the Python streaming snippet — note that you open a stream and then you can flush tokens as they arrive. (screen share) I'm pasting the code in chat.
[01:15] Priya: There is also the console toggle for streaming vs chunked; if you expect long responses, our batching + streaming combo reduces latency spikes.
[01:30] Samir: quick Q — for auth we prefer not to bake keys in images. what do you recommend for multi-env (dev/staging/prod) secrets?
[01:36] Priya: Good call. common patterns: 1) Use short-lived service tokens via your SSO (OIDC) and Redwood service accounts, 2) For CI -> use GitHub Actions secrets / OIDC to request Redwood token at runtime, 3) For local dev use .env with a dev key restricted by domain and rate. We showed the Github workflow template in the repo — I'll send that.
[02:10] Becky: And for local dev, is there a recommended revoke/rotate cadence?
[02:13] Priya: Rotate per project weekly/monthly depending on risk. For short-lived tokens you can do minutes to hours. We also support IP restrictions on keys for hosted customers.
[02:28] Jordan: moving on to TypeScript — Luca, any high-level differences to call out?
[02:33] Luca: TS SDK mirrors Python; promise/stream differences are idiomatic, but config and env handling are the same. We included examples for Next.js SSR/edge functions and for Vercel/Netlify deployments.
[02:50] Maya: we use Next.js, good. do you have examples for serverless cold-starts and KV cache warmup?
[02:56] Priya: we have a small pattern: pre-warm KV caches at deploy time with a background job and use prefix caching for common prompts. Optimize (console) will surface cache hits and advise cache TTLs.
[03:20] Samir: on the topic of Optimize, can you explain how the console suggests batching config? our traffic is bursty, and we want to minimize latency regressions.
[03:28] Priya: Sure. Optimize collects per-route token distributions and suggests continuous batching parameters — target batch size, max latency windows, and GPU grouping. there is also an autoscaling policy for dedicated pools. it will simulate cost impact in the console so you can weigh latency vs cost.
[03:50] Rajiv: security — KMS/HSM integration. we have an internal HSM and need Redwood to integrate or accept wrapped keys. what's supported?
[03:58] Luca: For Private customers we support customer KMS via our integration points (we can tunnel to your key proxy in VPC), for Hosted we provide envelope encryption with Redwood-managed KMS plus customer-managed keys in some tiers. For air-gapped or on-prem installs, there is an HSM connector. I'll log details in the follow-up.
[04:20] Rajiv: audit logs — retention and export?
[04:23] Jordan: console has token-level traceability and you can push logs to S3/Cloud Storage or a SIEM via webhook. retention and export are configurable per contract.
[04:32] Maya: is there any sample for how to run a small benchmark? our main metric is tail latency P95 for a 2k token generation across 4k context.
[04:40] Priya: we usually ask for sample prompts and sequence length distributions, then run 500-1k requests with your payload. we can simulate with dedicated vs hosted variants and return cost and latency—we did this for a customer with similar RAG patterns last month.
[04:58] Becky: about on-prem: our security team will likely want an air-gapped option, but we need the control plane still. what's your private deployment architecture?
[05:05] Luca: Private ships as two parts: customer-managed control plane that is reachable via VPC peering (or on-prem control plane) and a data plane that runs within your network. you can opt for no egress. we provide an installer and ansible/helm charts.
[05:24] Samir: how does model version pinning work across these? we need to pin to a quantized 4-bit variant for cost control.
[05:30] Priya: You can pin model versions at per-route level in the config. Redwood supports quantized variants and will fall back to compatible variants if there's capacity issues. Optimize can recommend quantization levels for your workload.
[05:48] [pause — screen share switches to quickstart repo]
[06:05] Priya: I'm going to run a live dev flow — local env, hydrate .env, run python example, then switch to TypeScript. bear with me if the video is choppy.
[06:20] [06:20] Priya: (typing) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_dev_*** — ok run server.
[06:30] Maya: while you run — does the SDK auto-retry on transient 503s or do we need to implement?
[06:36] Priya: SDK has built-in retry with exponential backoff and jitter. we also expose hooks for custom logic — e.g., you can inspect rate-limit headers and apply client-side pacing.
[06:50] Samir: what about token accounting for streaming — do partial tokens count?
[06:55] Jordan: tokens billed are final tokenization of the complete response; streaming doesn't double-bill but there are considerations for partial chunking overhead; we'll send the exact billing doc.
[07:10] Becky: CI examples? we use GitLab CI.
[07:13] Priya: repo has GitHub Actions example; for GitLab it's the same pattern: inject secrets via variables, prefer ephemeral tokens via OIDC. we included a sample script that requests a short-lived Redwood token using OIDC and then runs integration tests.
[07:30] Rajiv: SSO — can Redwood integrate with our Okta?
[07:34] Luca: Yes, SAML/Okta is supported for console + SSO for user management. service account auth can be bridged via OIDC.
[07:45] Maya: on the dev side — our app runs on multiple regions. is there region routing from Redwood? we want data residency for EU traffic.
[07:53] Jordan: Yes — smart routing rules can pin requests by geo or route to a specific region. Hosted supports regional endpoints and we also offer dedicated capacity in specific regions.
[08:10] Priya: Quick note on cost control — you can set token caps per API key and per-route spend limits, and Optimize will alert on quality regressions when switching quantization.
[08:25] Samir: can the SDK emit tracing spans that our APM can ingest?
[08:28] Priya: We support OpenTelemetry hooks; you can export traces to your APM. console also surfaces request-level traces for per-model slowdowns.
[08:40] [09:00] Maya: let's talk about the sample workload — we'll share a prompt set and the average/99th seq lengths. what format do you want?
[09:06] Priya: CSV with prompt, mean_tokens, max_tokens, and an example response is perfect. also indicate if you do retrieval steps (RAG) and the size of retrieved context.
[09:20] Becky: any gotchas for Next.js edge functions?
[09:24] Luca: edge functions need the lightweight runtime; we provide an edge client optimized for smaller bundles and lower cold-starts. avoid large KV preloads at cold start — warm with a background job.
[09:40] Samir: boundaries for dedicated vs hosted — at what throughput should we consider dedicated?
[09:45] Jordan: customers often move to dedicated when they want predictable latency and commit to monthly throughput. roughly if you're >X tokens/month or need guaranteed GPU pools, dedicated starts to make sense. we'll provide numbers tailored to your traffic in the follow-up.
[10:05] Rajiv: compliance — SOC 2 and ISO?
[10:08] Luca: We are SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO; we can share certs in the secure portal. also audit logs are available per contract.
[10:20] [11:00] Priya: switching to Optimize console — here are per-route analytics: token distribution, observed P95, and suggested batch sizes. the UI highlights routes with high unit cost and gives actionable toggles: enable KV cache, lower max tokens, or try quantized model.
[11:30] Maya: can we simulate rollback? what happens if a quantized model introduces hallucinations?
[11:35] Priya: We support canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies — you can set evaluation thresholds and if quality dips by X%, traffic flows back to the prior variant automatically. we also tie evals to prompt sets so you can measure hallucination rates.
[12:05] Becky: will Optimize give a cost delta before applying change?
[12:08] Priya: Yes, it shows estimated token cost delta and expected latency change.
[12:20] Samir: for the bench — are there infra constraints to run on our side or can Redwood run it?
[12:24] Jordan: We can run a bench on Redwood side if you provide sanitized prompts and a test IAM role, otherwise we'll provide the load harness for you to run.
[12:36] Maya: we prefer Redwood to run the first pass to save time — ok?
[12:40] Priya: absolutely, we'll need the prompt set and an S3 share or secure upload.
[12:50] [13:15] Jordan: let's capture open questions — Rajiv had KMS/HSM specifics, Maya had bench payload, Samir asked about region routing, Becky wants Next.js edge patterns. we'll assign owners.
[13:30] Rajiv: couple of clarifications — for private on-prem, is there a control plane dependency to Redwood cloud?
[13:36] Luca: you can choose a self-hosted control plane fully in your network for the air-gapped option, or a VPC-connected control plane. both supported.
[13:50] Maya: curious — any recommended quantization for Llama type models at 4-bit?
[13:54] Priya: 4-bit q4 variants usually keep quality pretty well for completions; Optimize will run an automatic A/B on your eval set to validate.
[14:10] [14:25] Becky: follow-up on billing: how are streaming tokens counted for embeddings + chat flows?
[14:30] Jordan: embeddings billed per embedding unit, chat per token with context + responses. we'll include a billing cheat sheet.
[14:45] Samir: can keys be scoped to route and env?
[14:48] Priya: yes, keys can be scoped to route, model, and environment, with per-key spend caps.
[15:00] [15:30] Jordan: quick demo done, time for Q&A and next steps.
[15:35] Maya: two last asks — share the Github Actions template and a sample Next.js edge snippet.
[15:40] Jordan: noted; Priya will send both.
[15:45] Rajiv: also, please include the security pack with KMS/HSM integration doc and SOC 2 artifacts.
[15:50] Luca: will attach security pack link in the follow-up.
[16:00] Becky: will you provide an initial estimate for hosted vs dedicated cost for our expected 10M tokens/month?
[16:06] Priya: yes we'll model both and include suggestions from Optimize to reduce unit cost.
[16:20] Jordan: recap of next steps and owners — we captured action items, we'll send calendar invite for the scoping call. any final questions?
[16:32] Maya: none, thanks everyone.
[16:36] Samir: good session, thanks.
[16:38] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up with repo and docs.
